newsitem.title: UK: British court victory for Harrods owners.
newsitem.headline: British court victory for Harrods owners.

text.p: The Egyptian-born Al Fayed brothers, owners of London's luxury Harrods department store, on Wednesday won a court battle against the British government's refusal to grant them citizenship.
Government officials responded by saying that Home Secretary (Interior Minister) Michael Howard would appeal to the House of Lords, Britain's highest court, against the brothers' court victory.
Appeal court judges ruled that Mohamed and his brother Ali had not been treated fairly because they had not been given the reasons for the refusal.
Judge Lord Woolf said: "They have not had the fairness to which they were entitled and the rule of law must be upheld."
The Al Fayeds, who have lived in Britain for 30 years, had appealed against a High Court decision that Home Secretary Howard acted lawfully in refusing their application to become British citizens.
If the appeal court's judgment is upheld, Howard will have to reconsider the Al Fayed brothers' application for naturalisation and give them the reasons for any subsequent refusal.
Harrods spokesman Michael Cole said the brothers had won a "great legal victory."
He added: "Mr Mohamed Al Fayed has lived here for 30 years without incurring so much as a parking ticket."
"He wanted simply to share the nationality of his four British children -- and he hopes now that, without further ado, the Home Secretary will grant him the passport which he has been denied."
Mohamed caused a storm in November 1994 when he alleged he had paid two junior government ministers to ask questions in parliament on his behalf. Both ministers resigned.
The row hit the headlines again last month when one of the former ministers sensationally dropped a libel action connected with the case.
The brothers' applications for British citizenship were submitted 13 months apart but were refused on February 23 last year. The Fayeds' children are British citizens, as is Ali's wife.

Mohamed believes that the British "establishment" has conspired against him and that the government's refusal to grant him and his brother citizenship is based on prejudice that ignores the contribution he has made to British life.

But after the brothers took over the House of Fraser, which controlled Harrods, government inspectors concluded in 1990 that they had "dishonestly misrepresented their origins, their wealth, their business interests and their resources."
